They consult a thesaurus and consider options like "valiant," "intrepid," and "audacious," ultimately choosing the word that best reflects the specific type of bravery exhibited by the character.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can identify synonyms and antonyms for common words. I can use synonyms to avoid repetition in my writing and antonyms to show contrast between ideas.
Ex. A student is writing a report about the rainforest and wants to vary their word choice instead of repeating "big" several times. They use a thesaurus to find synonyms like "massive," "enormous," and "gigantic" to make their writing more interesting and precise.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify words that mean the same thing (synonyms) and words that mean the opposite (antonyms). I am learning to use synonyms and antonyms in my writing.
Ex. A student is working on a vocabulary list with the words "happy" and "sad." They can identify "joyful" as a synonym for "happy" and "dejected" as an antonym for "happy."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I am learning about synonyms and antonyms. I can match words that have the same or opposite meanings.
Ex. A student is given a worksheet with pairs of words, such as "hot/cold" and "big/small." They can successfully match the pairs as antonyms.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can communicate effectively with peers and adults.
I can communicate reactions to statements made by others.
I can answer questions from peers and adults about self or joint activities.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can communicate with adults.
I can respond when addressed by an adult.
I can answer questions from adults about self or current activity.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can use words, pictures, symbols, or sign to communicate.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.3.c|4.descriptor_flag: School descriptor may not match this standard

descriptors_suggested.cc_advanced: I can choose precise synonyms and antonyms to make my writing more exact and interesting.
descriptors_suggested.cc_at_target: I can understand words by relating them to their synonyms and antonyms.
descriptors_suggested.cc_approaching: I can match a word to a synonym or antonym using a chart.
descriptors_suggested.cc_emerging: I can match a word to its opposite picture with help.
descriptors_suggested.ee_at_target: I can show I understand opposites, such as hot and cold.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.3.c|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.3.d|4.text: Make connections between words and how they are used in real life (i.e., help students build or add onto existing schema when encountering new words).
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.3.d|4.ee_text: Identify words that describe personal emotional states.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can actively connect new words and concepts to my prior knowledge and experiences, creating meaningful associations that deepen my understanding and retention. I can analyze how word choices reflect different perspectives, contexts, and purposes in real-world communication.
Ex. A student learning the word "migration" in a science unit on birds can connect it to their family's annual summer vacation trip, understanding that both involve a temporary movement from one place to another. They can further analyze how "migration" is used differently in social studies to describe human movements.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can relate new words to things I already know. I can use my own experiences and background knowledge to understand the meaning of unfamiliar words.
Ex. A student encounters the word "architect" in a book about famous buildings. They connect it to their uncle, who designs houses, and can now visualize an architect's role in creating structures.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can sometimes make connections between new words and things I have seen or done. I am learning to use my own experiences to understand new words.
Ex. A student learning the word "generous" hears a story about a child sharing their toys. With some prompting, they can connect the character's actions to the word and understand that "generous" means being willing to share.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I am learning to connect words to pictures and objects. I am starting to understand that words have meanings related to the world around me.
Ex. A student learning the word "transportation" is shown pictures of cars, buses, and airplanes. They can start to connect the word to different ways people move from place to place.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can identify and understand words that describe different feelings. I can use these words to talk about my own emotions and the emotions of others.
I can accurately identify words like "frustrated," "excited," "disappointed," and "proud" as words that describe feelings. They can use these words to talk about their own emotional experiences and to infer the feelings of characters in stories.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can identify words that describe basic feelings like happy, sad, mad, and scared. I am learning more words that describe different emotions.
I can match facial expressions to basic emotion words. They are beginning to recognize and use a wider range of emotion vocabulary, such as "surprised," "nervous," or "silly."
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can show how I feel with my face and body. I am learning words to name different feelings.
I can express my emotions through facial expressions, body language, and vocal tone. They are beginning to associate these expressions with basic emotion words like "happy," "sad," "mad," and "scared."

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.3.d|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.4.a|4.text: Demonstrate an ability to collaboratively and independently build vocabulary knowledge when encountering unknown words including cultural, general academic, and discipline-specific terms and phrases; use vocabulary appropriate to the context and situation. a. Identify and use phrases that signal precise actions, emotions, or states of being (e.g., quizzed, whined, stammered) and that are basic to a particular topic (e.g., wildlife, conservation, and endangered when discussing animal preservation).
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.4.a|4.ee_text: Use words acquired through conversations, being read to, and during shared reading activities a. Identify key domain-specific vocabulary

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can strategically choose and use precise verbs, adverbs, and descriptive phrases to create vivid imagery, convey nuanced emotions, and enhance the clarity and impact of my writing and speaking. I can confidently incorporate domain-specific vocabulary to demonstrate my understanding of a topic and engage my audience effectively.
Ex. In a persuasive essay about protecting endangered species, a student writes, "Poachers ruthlessly hunt elephants for their ivory tusks, decimating populations and pushing these magnificent creatures to the brink of extinction." The student's use of strong verbs like "ruthlessly" and "decimating" and domain-specific terms like "poachers," "ivory tusks," and "endangered species" demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the topic and creates a powerful emotional appeal.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can identify and use words and phrases that describe specific actions, feelings, or states of being. I can use vocabulary related to a topic to show my understanding.
Ex. When writing a story about a nervous character, a student might use verbs like "fidget," "tremble," and "stammer" instead of more general words like "move" or "talk." When discussing a science unit on weather, they accurately use terms like "precipitation," "evaporation," and "condensation."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can choose words that describe actions, feelings, or states of being. I am learning to use more specific and interesting words in my writing and speaking.
Ex. Instead of writing "The dog was happy," a student might write "The dog wagged its tail excitedly." They are beginning to use more descriptive verbs to show rather than tell.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can use different words to describe how people are feeling or what they are doing. I am learning new words related to different topics we are studying.
Ex. A student can identify "giggled" as a way to show someone is happy and "cried" as a way to show someone is sad. They are starting to build a vocabulary of words related to specific subjects, like using "habitat" and "ecosystem" in a science lesson.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use context as a clue to guide the selection of a word that completes a sentence read aloud by an adult.
I can select from choices a word to complete a sentence (e.g., The teacher reads a sentence aloud skips one word and asks students to select the missing word from an array of choices.).
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can use context as a clue to guide the selection of a word that completes a familiar sentence read aloud by an adult. 
I can while listening to a familiar text read aloud, select an appropriate word from choices (e.g., The teacher pauses and offers choices of words that will complete the sentence. Student selects the appropriate word.).
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can make choices among familiar words to complete familiar sentences.
I can complete the sentence, “I want <missing word> for lunch.”
I can choose a contextually correct picture to represent an answer to a question about a familiar passage.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.4.a|4.descriptor_flag: School descriptor may not match this standard

descriptors_suggested.cc_advanced: I can use precise action words and topic words accurately in my speaking and writing.
descriptors_suggested.cc_at_target: I can learn and use words that show precise actions and feelings and words basic to a topic.
descriptors_suggested.cc_approaching: I can use topic words from a word wall in my writing with support.
descriptors_suggested.cc_emerging: I can point to a picture of a topic word with help.
descriptors_suggested.ee_at_target: I can identify key subject-specific words.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.4.a|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.a|4.text: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English grammar and usage when writing or speaking. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English. Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with: a. relative pronouns and adverbs;
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.a|4.ee_text: Demonstrate standardized English grammar and usage when communicating. a. Use possessive pronouns.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can easily change how I talk and write depending on who I'm talking to and what I'm writing about. I can explain why different types of writing and speaking require different ways of using language.
Ex. A student gives a presentation to the class about their favorite hobby, using more formal language and avoiding slang. Later, they write a note to a friend about a funny event at recess, using informal language and humor. They can explain that they adjusted their language to fit the audience and purpose.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use the correct grammar and punctuation when I write and speak for different situations. I can choose the right words and phrases to make my meaning clear.
Ex. A student writes a story using correct punctuation, capitalization, and grammar. They use different types of sentences (simple, compound, complex) to make their writing interesting.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I am learning to use the right grammar and punctuation when I write and speak. I am getting better at choosing words that fit the situation.
Ex. A student is learning to use commas in a series and to capitalize proper nouns. They are starting to use more descriptive words in their writing, but sometimes they still choose words that don't quite fit.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I am learning about grammar and punctuation. I am starting to understand that we use different kinds of words when we write and speak.
Ex. A student can identify the beginning and end of a sentence. They are learning about different parts of speech, like nouns and verbs.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use many different grammar rules to write clear and interesting sentences.
Example: "My dog, Sparky, is smaller than my neighbor's dog, but Sparky runs faster than any dog I know!"
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can write simple sentences and am learning to use more interesting words to compare things and show how they are related.
Example: "My dog is small. He runs fast!"
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I am learning about how to build sentences and can use some words to talk about who owns things, where things are, and compare things.
Example: "My dog. Run fast!"

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.a|4.descriptor_flag: School descriptor may not match this standard

descriptors_suggested.cc_advanced: I can use relative pronouns and adverbs to combine ideas into complex sentences and explain their purpose.
descriptors_suggested.cc_at_target: I can use relative pronouns (who, which, that) and relative adverbs (where, when, why) correctly.
descriptors_suggested.cc_approaching: I can join two sentences with who or which using a model.
descriptors_suggested.cc_emerging: I can answer a who question about a picture with help.
descriptors_suggested.ee_at_target: I can use possessive pronouns such as my, your, his and her.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.a|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.b|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with prepositional phrases;
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.b|4.ee_text: Combine common nouns with verbs, nouns, or pronouns in communication

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can use prepositional phrases like "under the table" or "before the game" in my writing, and explain how they show where or when something happens.
I can create complex sentences using prepositional phrases to add detail.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use prepositional phrases like "on the chair" or "after school" in my writing.
I can explain how prepositional phrases describe where or when something happens.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can use simple prepositional phrases like "on the desk" or "at home" with help.
I can explain with support how a prepositional phrase tells where or when.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can recognize and use basic prepositional phrases like "in the room" with help.
I can try to explain what a prepositional phrase shows with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use nouns and verbs together to make sentences, like “The cat runs.”
I can combine nouns with pronouns or other nouns to talk about people, animals, or things.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can use a noun and a verb together, like “boy run,” with help.
I can say or point to two words, like a noun and a pronoun, when talking with guidance.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can say or point to a noun and verb together, like “boy eat,” with support.
I can use pictures or words to put two things together, like “boy” and “him,” with help.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.b|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.c|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with order of adjective

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can correctly use multiple adjectives in the right order, such as "a big red balloon," and explain why they are in that order.
I can vary my use of adjectives to make my writing more descriptive and accurate.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use adjectives in the correct order, such as "a small blue car," in my writing.
I can explain the proper order for adjectives, such as size before color.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can use two adjectives like "big" and "yellow" in my writing with help, and I can try to put them in the right order (e.g., "a big yellow ball").
I can explain the order of adjectives with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can use simple adjectives like "big" and "small" in my writing with help (e.g., "a small dog").
I can try to put two adjectives together with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.c|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.d|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with adjectives, adverbs, conjunctions;
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.d|4.ee_text: Use comparative and superlative adjectives to describe people or objects.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use adjectives, adverbs, and conjunctions to create detailed sentences and explain why they make my writing clearer (e.g., "I used 'quickly' to describe how fast she ran and 'because' to connect two ideas").
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use adjectives, adverbs, and conjunctions to make my writing more interesting (e.g., "I used 'happily' to describe how he smiled, and 'but' to join two ideas").
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use simple adjectives, adverbs, and conjunctions in sentences with help (e.g., "I wrote 'softly' to show how the wind blew and used 'and' to join two ideas").
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use basic adjectives and conjunctions like "and" or "but" in my writing with help (e.g., "I said 'big' and 'red' to describe a ball and used 'and' to join two sentences").
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use words like “bigger” or “biggest” to compare people or objects.
I can describe things by comparing them with words like “taller” or “shortest.”
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can say or point to a word that compares two things, like “bigger,” with help.
I can use simple comparing words, like “big” and “bigger,” with guidance.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can listen to or repeat words that compare two things, like “big” and “bigger,” with support.
I can point to or say one word that compares two things with help.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.d|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.e|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with compound and complex sentences
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.e|4.ee_text: Use common prepositions (e.g., to, from, in, out, on, off, by, with).

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can use compound and complex sentences in my writing, such as "I went to the park, and I played soccer because it was sunny," and explain how they make my writing more detailed.
I can connect multiple ideas in one sentence using conjunctions like "because" or "although" to show relationships between ideas.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can write compound and complex sentences to join ideas together (e.g., "I ate lunch, and then I did my homework").
I can explain how I use conjunctions like "and," "but," or "because" to make longer sentences.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can try to write sentences with "and" or "because" to join ideas with help (e.g., "I like pizza, and I like burgers").
I can explain with guidance how combining sentences makes my writing clearer.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can use simple conjunctions like "and" to join two sentences with help (e.g., "I ran, and I jumped").
I can try to use conjunctions to connect ideas when someone supports me.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use words like “in,” “on,” or “with” to tell where things are or how they are used.
I can put prepositions in sentences to describe where things are, like “The book is on the table.”
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can use words like “in” or “on” to tell where something is with help.
I can point to or say a preposition, like “with” or “by,” in a sentence with guidance.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can point to something “in” or “on” a picture when asked with support.
I can say or repeat a common preposition, like “in” or “on,” with help.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.e|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.f|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with easily confused words (e.g., to, too, two).
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.f|4.ee_text: Combine three or more words in communication.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can correctly use and explain the difference between confusing words like "to," "too," and "two" in my writing (e.g., "I went to the store" vs. "I ate too much cake").
I can make sure to choose the correct word based on the context of my sentence.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use words like "to," "too," and "two" correctly in my writing (e.g., "I went to the park" vs. "I have two cats").
I can explain the difference between confusing words when writing sentences.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can use some confusing words like "to" and "too" in sentences with help (e.g., "I went to school" and "I like pizza too").
I can try to explain the difference between confusing words with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can recognize words that sound the same but are spelt differently, like "to" and "two," with help.
I can try to use these words in simple sentences when someone helps me.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use three or more words to make a sentence, like “The dog is running.”
I can combine words to say or write a complete thought.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can say or point to three words together, like “big dog run,” with help.
I can use three words in a simple sentence with guidance.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can combine two or three words, like “dog run fast,” with support.
I can point to or say three words to describe something with help.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.5.f|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.a|4.text: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English. Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with: a. capitalization,
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.a|4.ee_text: Demonstrate understanding of conventions of standardized English. a. Capitalize the first word in a sentence.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can use capitalization, punctuation, and spelling correctly in my writing to make my meaning clear and follow the rules of standard English. I can explain why these rules are important and how they help readers understand my writing.
Ex. A student writes a report about a historical event, correctly using commas to separate items in a series, commas after introductory phrases, and quotation marks around direct quotes. They can explain that using quotation marks accurately gives credit to the original speaker and helps avoid plagiarism.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use capital letters, commas, and quotation marks correctly in my writing. I can spell most grade-level words correctly and use a dictionary or other resources when I need help spelling.
Ex. A student writes a narrative story using correct capitalization for proper nouns, dialogue punctuation, and commas in compound sentences. They can spell most words correctly and use a dictionary to check the spelling of words they are unsure about.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I am learning to use capital letters, commas, and quotation marks in my writing. I am getting better at spelling grade-level words, and I am learning to use a dictionary for help.
Ex. A student is learning to use commas in compound sentences and to capitalize the first word of a sentence. They are becoming more aware of spelling patterns and can use a dictionary to look up words, although they may need help finding the correct spelling.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I am learning about capital letters, periods, and question marks. I am starting to learn how to spell grade-level words.
Ex. A student can identify the beginning and end of a sentence and use a period or question mark correctly. They are learning to recognize and write their first and last names correctly and are starting to learn basic spelling rules.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use capital letters at the beginning of sentences and spell words correctly using what I know about sounds and letters.
Example: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I usually remember to use capital letters at the beginning of sentences. I am getting better at spelling words correctly by sounding them out and using spelling patterns.
Example: "The quick brown fox jumped over the laze dog."
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I am learning to start sentences with a capital letter. I am starting to spell some words correctly by thinking about the sounds I hear.
Example: "the qik fox run."

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.a|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.b|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with commas and quotation marks for quotations,.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can use commas and quotation marks correctly when writing dialogue, such as "He said, 'Let's go to the park,'" and explain why they are used.
I can easily identify and correct errors in dialogue punctuation in my writing.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use commas and quotation marks correctly when quoting someone in my writing (e.g., "She said, 'I love reading'").
I can explain why I use quotation marks and commas to show dialogue.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can use quotation marks and commas with some help when writing what someone says (e.g., "He said, 'I like ice cream'").
I can try to explain why quotation marks are used when quoting someone with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can try to use quotation marks and commas when someone helps me write what someone says (e.g., "With help, I wrote, 'She said, "Come here"'").
I can try to add punctuation to show when someone is talking in my writing with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.b|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.c|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with commas in compound sentences

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can use commas correctly in compound sentences, like "I finished my homework, and then I played outside," and explain why the comma is needed.
I can easily identify and correct missing commas in compound sentences in my writing.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use commas correctly to join two ideas in a compound sentence (e.g., "I went to the park, and I played soccer").
I can explain why I use a comma before conjunctions like "and" or "but" in a compound sentence.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can use commas in compound sentences with some help (e.g., "I cleaned my room, and I watched TV").
I can try to explain why I use a comma in a compound sentence with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can try to use commas when joining two simple sentences with help (e.g., "I ate lunch, and I went to school").
I can try to understand where to place a comma in a sentence when someone supports me.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.c|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.d|4.text: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with spell grade-level words correctly using reference materials to solve words as needed
WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.d|4.ee_text: Spell words phonetically, drawing on knowledge of letter- sound relationships, and/or common spelling patterns.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can spell grade-level words correctly without help and use a dictionary to check when needed (e.g., "I spelled 'beautiful' correctly and used a dictionary to check 'necessary'").
I can use reference materials like a dictionary or spell checker to correct my spelling errors.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can spell grade-level words correctly in my writing (e.g., "I spelled 'animal' and 'teacher' correctly").
I can use a dictionary or other tools to help me spell words I don't know.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can spell common grade-level words with help (e.g., "I spelled 'happy' and 'house' correctly with guidance").
I can try to use a dictionary or spell checker with support when I am unsure of a word's spelling.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can try to spell simple words correctly with help (e.g., "I spelled 'cat' and 'dog' with support").
I can try to use a dictionary or get help to spell words I don't know.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can spell words by sounding them out, using what I know about letters and sounds.
I can use common spelling patterns, like “CVC,” to spell simple words.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can try to spell words by saying the sounds I hear with help.
I can write letters that match sounds in words with guidance.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can listen to a word and say or write one of the sounds I hear with support.
I can use pictures or letters to show how a word sounds with help.

WI-CC-ELA|L.4.6.d|4.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.3|5.text: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words. a. Use combined knowledge of all letter-sound correspondences, syllabication patterns, and morphology (e.g., roots and affixes) to read accurately unfamiliar multisyllabic words in context and out of context.
WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.3|5.ee_text: Use letter-sound knowledge to read words. a. Decode and encode common sight words and single syllable words.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can sound out and figure out the meanings of long, difficult words, even if I've never seen them before! I can break down words into smaller parts, like prefixes, suffixes, and root words, to understand what they mean.
Ex: A student comes across the word "biodiversity" in a science article. They recognize the parts "bio" (meaning life) and "diversity" (meaning variety) and correctly infer that the word means "the variety of life."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can sound out and figure out the meanings of most multi-syllable words. I can break words into syllables and use what I know about prefixes, suffixes, and root words to help me read and understand new words.
Ex: When reading about ancient history, a student encounters the word "hieroglyphics." They break it into syllables (hi-er-o-glyph-ics) to decode it and understand it refers to a system of writing.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can sound out and figure out the meanings of longer words, but I might need some help with really tricky ones. I'm getting better at breaking words into parts and using prefixes and suffixes to help me read.
Ex: A student pauses at the word "prehistoric" in a book. They recognize the prefix "pre-" meaning "before" and can connect it to the word "history" to understand the word's meaning.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can sound out longer words and figuring out what they mean. I'm learning how to break words into smaller parts to make them easier to read.
Ex: When encountering the word "rebuild" in a text, a student might sound out each individual sound ("r-e-b-uild") and, with some prompting, recognize the prefix "re-" signifies doing something again.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can sound out and read words with two or three syllables. I am learning to use what I know about letters and sounds, along with parts of words, to help me read new words.
Ex: A student encounters the word "watermelon" in a story. They can break it into syllables (wa-ter-mel-on), decode each syllable, and blend them together to read the word.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can sound out and read some words with two syllables. I am learning more about how letters and sounds work together. I am starting to learn about parts of words.
Ex: A student encounters the word "sunshine" in a text. They can break it into its component parts ("sun" and "shine"), decode each syllable, and understand the combined meaning.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can sound out words with two syllables. I am learning the sounds that letters make. I am starting to put sounds together to read words.
Ex: A student is presented with the word "in" on a flashcard and can correctly identify the sounds the letters "i" and "n" make. They can then blend those sounds to read the word.

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.3|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.a|5.text: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension. a. Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.a|5.ee_text: Read words in text. Read text comprised of familiar words with accuracy and understanding. a. Use features of print to identify or verbalize appropriate expression while reading familiar texts.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can read and understand challenging texts at my grade level. I can read smoothly and with expression, like I'm talking. I can figure out the meanings of new words and use my reading skills to learn new information and complete tasks. I enjoy reading different types of books and articles.
Ex: A student effortlessly reads aloud a passage from a historical fiction novel, using appropriate pacing, tone, and inflection to convey the characters' emotions and the scene's mood. They can readily answer comprehension questions about the text's deeper meaning and themes.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can read and understand texts at my grade level. I can read smoothly and with expression. I can figure out the meanings of new words and use what I read to learn new things. I can read aloud clearly so others can understand.
Ex: When encountering an unfamiliar scientific term in a nonfiction article, a student uses context clues within the surrounding sentences to infer the word's meaning and continues reading smoothly.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can read most texts at my grade level. I can read smoothly sometimes, but I might still need to reread some parts to understand them. I can figure out some new words as I read.
Ex: A student pauses occasionally while reading a chapter from a grade-level novel to reread a sentence with an unfamiliar word. They attempt to sound out the word and use context clues to determine its meaning.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I am working on reading texts at my grade level. I am still learning to read smoothly and accurately. I sometimes need help figuring out new words.
Ex: A student, when asked to read aloud a short paragraph from a grade-level text, may read slowly, word by word, and have difficulty decoding multi-syllable words or using punctuation to guide their phrasing and intonation.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can read texts that have familiar words. I can read smoothly and with expression. When I come across a word I don't know, I can use what I know about letters and sounds, along with clues from the sentence, to figure it out.
Ex: A student is reading a story about a cat and comes across the word "purring." The student uses their knowledge of letter sounds to decode the word and confirms its meaning by connecting it to the cat's happy feeling in the story.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can read some texts that have familiar words. I can use what I know about letters and sounds to help me read words. When I come across a word I don't know, I can use clues from the pictures or the sentences to try and figure it out.
Ex: A student is reading a text about animals on a farm and encounters the word "neigh." They may not be able to decode it independently but can use a picture of a horse to infer the word's meaning.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I am learning to read words in stories and books. I am learning to use the pictures to help me understand the words. I am getting better at sounding out words I don't know.
Ex: A student is reading a simple sentence like "The dog is brown." They can point to each word as they read it and use the picture of the brown dog to confirm the meaning of the word "brown."

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.a|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.b|5.text: Read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.b|5.ee_text: Use letter-sound knowledge and context to confirm or self-correct word recognition when reading.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can read grade-level text fluently, with accurate expression and pacing, making it sound natural (e.g., "I read a chapter of the book aloud using different voices for each character").
I can improve my reading rate and expression with each practice, making fewer mistakes (e.g., "I reread the passage with better pauses and emotions").
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can read grade-level text with good accuracy and expression (e.g., "I read the dialogue in the story aloud with the right speed and feeling").
I can improve my reading after practicing a text several times (e.g., "After reading it again, I used better expression in my voice").
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can read aloud with some expression and accuracy but may need help adjusting my speed (e.g., "I read the text aloud but needed help slowing down in some parts").
I can improve my reading with practice and guidance (e.g., "I sounded more fluent after practicing with help").
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can read aloud with support, improving my speed and expression with practice (e.g., "With help, I read the passage and used more pauses to sound clearer").
I can try to read more smoothly when practicing multiple times (e.g., "I practiced reading the text aloud and got better with each try").
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can use the sounds of letters and clues from the story to check if a word is correct when I read.
I can fix a word I read wrong by using what I know about letter sounds and what makes sense in the story.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can sound out a word and use pictures or other words in the story to help me figure out if it is correct with help.
I can try to correct a word I don’t know using the first letter and clues from the story with guidance.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can listen to the sounds in a word and use a picture or clue from the story to understand it with support.
I can recognize the first sound of a word and check the picture to help me read with help.

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.b|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.c|5.text: Use context to confirm or self- correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can quickly use context clues to figure out unfamiliar words and confirm their meanings without needing to reread (e.g., "I knew 'accelerate' meant to go faster because of the other words around it").
I can reread parts of the text to make sure I understand unfamiliar words and correct mistakes (e.g., "I reread the sentence to confirm that 'evaporate' means to disappear as steam").
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can use context clues to figure out or correct the meaning of a word while reading (e.g., "I used the other words in the paragraph to understand that 'glimpse' means a quick look").
I can reread parts of the text to help me understand difficult words (e.g., "I reread the paragraph to confirm that 'stumble' meant to trip").
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can use context clues with some help to figure out or correct word meanings (e.g., "I used other words in the sentence to guess that 'burst' means to pop").
I can reread parts of a sentence with support to better understand a word (e.g., "With help, I reread the sentence to understand 'rare' means uncommon").
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can recognize when I need help with a word’s meaning and ask for assistance (e.g., "I asked for help when I wasn’t sure if 'delicate' meant fragile or strong").
I can try to reread a word or sentence with help to confirm the meaning (e.g., "With help, I reread the sentence and learned that 'quick' means fast").
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not Applicable.

WI-CC-ELA|RF.5.4.c|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.1|5.text: Locate and refer to relevant details and evidence when explaining what a text says explicitly or implicitly and make logical inferences. (RI&RL)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.1|5.ee_text: Identify explicit details in a text. (RI&RL)

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can analyze how an author uses specific details and evidence to support their ideas. I can make complex inferences about what a text means but doesn't say directly, considering different perspectives and interpretations. I can even use my understanding of a text to think about real-life situations and my own experiences.
Ex: After reading a biography about Harriet Tubman, a student infers that Tubman’s strong sense of empathy motivated her to risk her own safety to help others escape slavery, citing evidence from the text about her own experiences and actions.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can find important details and evidence in a text and use them to answer questions. I can make logical inferences about what a text means, even when the information isn't stated directly.
Ex: While reading a science article about the layers of the rainforest, a student connects details from different paragraphs to understand how each layer is interconnected, even though this relationship isn't stated directly.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can find most details and evidence in a text and use them to answer questions. I can make some inferences about what a text means, but I might need help understanding more complex inferences.
Ex: After reading a historical account of the American Revolution, a student can identify the main events that led to the war but might need guidance to understand the colonists' different perspectives on those events.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can find some details and evidence in a text and use them to answer questions. I can sometimes make basic inferences about what a text means.
Ex: After reading a short story about a child who is nervous about performing in a school play, a student can identify clues from the text that show the character is nervous, such as "His palms were sweaty" or "He kept forgetting his lines."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can identify and recall key details and information directly stated in a text. 
I can answer basic comprehension questions using explicit textual evidence.
Example: "The cat is fluffy, and it's sitting on a mat. The text says the cat purrs loudly because it's happy."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can select words or phrases from the text that provide clues about the meaning, even if the connection isn't fully formed. 
I can use picture and context clues to make simple inferences.
Example: (Teacher asks: "How do we know the cat likes the mat?") Student: "It says 'soft mat' and 'purred loudly.'"
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can identify words, pictures, or phrases in the text when prompted with simple, direct questions about explicit information.
Example: (Teacher points to the word "cat" in the text) "Can you find this word in the text? What word tells us what the cat is doing?" Student: (points to "sat") "Sat."

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.1|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.2|5.text: Summarize texts, from a variety of genres, to determine a theme or central idea and explain how it is supported by key details. (RI&RL)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.2|5.ee_text: Identify the theme or main idea from a text when it is not explicitly stated. (RI&RL)

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write a clear summary that explains how several key details work together to develop a theme or central idea.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can summarize a text and determine its theme or central idea and explain how key details support it.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify some key details in a text and begin to understand the main idea or theme, but I need help explaining how the details support it. 
Example: "The book The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe is about four kids who find a magical world inside a wardrobe. There's a mean witch who turns things to stone and a lion named Aslan who is good. I think the main idea is about being brave, but I'm not sure how Aslan coming back to life shows that."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can identify some key details in a short text, but I struggle to understand the main idea or theme. 
Example: "The book is about a lion named Aslan. There's a witch too. They go to a place called Narnia. It's cold there."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can dentify some key details in a text and begin to understand the main idea or theme but I need help explaining how the details support it.
 I can identify the main idea of a text with support from the teacher or a partner.
Example: "The book The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe is about four kids who find a magical world inside a wardrobe. There's a mean witch who turns things to stone and a lion named Aslan who is good. I think the main idea is about being brave, but I'm not sure how Aslan coming back to life shows that."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I require extensive support to identify the main idea or theme.
I may be able to identify key characters or events in a story with prompting.
Example: (Teacher points to a picture of Aslan) "Who is this?" ... "Can you say Aslan?"... (Teacher points to a picture of the White Witch) "And who is this?"
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I demonstrate an understanding of the basic elements of a story, such as characters and events, and I can answer simple questions about them with support. 
I may be able to retell a familiar story with prompting, using key words or phrases.
Example: (After listening to the teacher read The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe) Teacher: "Who went to Narnia?" Student: "The children." Teacher: "Yes, and who did they meet in Narnia?" Student: "Aslan... and the witch."

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.2|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.3|5.text: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, and events, drawing on specific details in the text. (RL) Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts based on specific evidence from the text. (RI)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.3|5.ee_text: Compare two characters in a familiar story. (RL) Compare two individuals, events or ideas in a text. (RI)

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can analyze the nuances of character, setting, and event interactions, explaining how these relationships contribute to the overall meaning and impact of the text. 
I can apply comparative analysis to complex real-world situations. 
Example: "While both Charlotte and Wilbur fear death, their reactions differ significantly. Charlotte, drawing on her experience and wisdom, faces her mortality with a sense of peace, focusing on helping Wilbur. This contrasts with Wilbur's panic and desperation, highlighting his innocence and need for guidance. This difference emphasizes the novel's themes of friendship, sacrifice, and the cycle of life."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can effectively compares and contrasts characters, settings, or events using specific details from the text. 
I clearly explains the relationships and interactions between story elements, supporting claims with textual evidence.
Example: "Charlotte and Templeton have a complex relationship. Charlotte is kind and helpful, shown when she writes words in her web to save Wilbur. Templeton is selfish and only helps when there's something in it for him, like getting to eat leftover fair food. This shows that even though they're different, they need each other."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identifies similarities and differences between characters, settings, or events but may struggle to provide specific textual details or explain the significance of the comparison. 
Example: "Wilbur and Fern are both different from the other characters. Wilbur is a pig, and Fern is a girl, so they are not alike. But they both care about each other."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can identify a single difference or similarity between two characters, settings, or events when explicitly prompted, but may not be able to elaborate or provide textual support. 
Example: (Teacher points to pictures of Wilbur and Charlotte) "How are Wilbur and Charlotte different?" Student: "Wilbur is a pig, and Charlotte is a spider."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can compare two characters, individuals, events, or ideas in a simple or short story. 
I can identify clear similarities and differences and provide some basic textual support for their claims. Example: "The tortoise and the hare are different. The hare is fast, but the tortoise is slow. The story says the hare ran quickly and took a nap. The tortoise went slow and steady and won the race."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can make basic connections between two individuals or events/actions in a simple or short story with support from the teacher or a partner. 
I may rely on picture clues and context to identify relationships. 
Example: (Teacher points to a picture of the hare sleeping) "What is the hare doing?" Student: "Sleeping." (Teacher points to a picture of the tortoise crossing the finish line) "Who won the race?" Student: "The tortoise."
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can demonstrate an understanding of who the characters are in a familiar, simple or short story and can answer simple questions about them with support. 
Example: (After listening to the teacher read The Tortoise and the Hare) Teacher: "Who was very fast?" Student: "The hare." Teacher: "And who was very slow?" Student: "The tortoise."

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.3|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.4|5.text: Determine the meaning of words, phrases, figurative language, academic and content-specific words, and analyze their effect on meaning, tone, and mood within a text. (RI&RL)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.4|5.ee_text: Determine the intended meaning of multimeaning and domain-specific words and phrases. (RI&RL)

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can analyze how the author's use of language, including figurative language, creates specific effects and contributes to the overall meaning, tone, and mood of a text, and I can apply this understanding to real-world examples of writing.
Example: "Palacio uses the metaphor 'August is a lamb to the slaughter' to show how unprepared he feels going into middle school. This creates a sympathetic tone and a mood of anxiety, making the reader feel worried for August. This kind of metaphor is effective because it creates a strong image in the reader's mind."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can determine the meaning of words, phrases, figurative language, and subject-specific vocabulary within a text. 
I can explain how these elements contribute to the overall meaning, tone, and mood. 
Example: "When Via says 'August is the Sun,' it means he's the center of attention in their family. This metaphor helps me understand how much Via cares about August and how his needs often come first."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify some examples of figurative language within a text and provide a basic explanation of their literal meaning. 
I may need support to connect figurative language to tone or mood. 
Example: "The author says August's face is 'like a Picasso painting.' That's a simile because it uses 'like.' I think it means his face is unusual."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can identify basic words and phrases within a text when explicitly guided. 
I may be able to decode and pronounce words but struggle with understanding their meaning in context.
Example: (Teacher points to the sentence "August was nervous about starting middle school.") "Can you read this sentence? ... What word tells us how August felt?"
descriptors.ee_at_target: Determines the meaning of some multi-meaning words and domain-specific phrases in a text using context clues. May need support with less familiar terms. Example: "I think 'heavy precipitation' means a lot of rain or snow is happening. The text talked about floods after heavy precipitation, so it must be a lot of water falling."
descriptors.ee_approaching: Identifies domain-specific words and phrases in a text with support from the teacher or visual aids. Can demonstrate understanding of basic meanings with prompting. Example: (Teacher points to the phrase "heavy precipitation" in the text) "Can you find this phrase in the text? What do you think it means?" Student: "Hmm, maybe a lot of rain?"
descriptors.ee_emerging: Identifies familiar words and phrases in a text with support. May need picture clues, repeated readings, or direct guidance to connect words to their meanings. Example: (Teacher points to a picture of heavy rain in the text) "What is this picture showing? Can you find the words in the text that match this picture?" Student (pointing to "heavy precipitation"): "Here!"

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.4|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.5|5.text: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to determine the overall structure of a story, drama, or poem. (RL) Compare and contrast the overall structure in two or more texts using terms such as sequence, comparison, cause and effect, and problem and solution. (RI)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.5|5.ee_text: With guidance and support, identify a story element that undergoes change from beginning to end (RL) and determine if a text tells about events, gives directions, or provides information on a topic (RI).

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can analyze how the structure of a text (like the order of chapters or the use of flashbacks) helps the author achieve their purpose. I can compare and contrast how different texts use structure to create different effects, like suspense or humor.
Ex: "The poem uses stanzas to group related ideas and create a sense of rhythm. The stanzas about the speaker's childhood are shorter and simpler, reflecting the innocence of that time, while the stanzas about adulthood are longer and more complex."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can explain how a story is organized, such as by using a timeline, flashbacks, or parallel plots. I can compare and contrast how two texts are structured, using terms like "problem and solution" or "cause and effect."
Ex: "This mystery story uses a flashback to show what happened before the crime, which helps create suspense. In contrast, this biography uses a chronological timeline to show the person's life."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify the beginning, middle, and end of a story and explain how the events are connected. I can recognize if a story is told in order or if it jumps around in time.
Ex: "The first chapter introduces the characters and setting. In the middle, the main character faces a challenge. The story ends with the problem being solved."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can retell the main events of a story in the order they happened.
Ex: "First, the family went on a trip. Then, they saw a bear. Finally, they went home."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can with support, identify a basic change in a story element from beginning to end and can sort different types of texts (stories, directions, information).
Example: (Teacher, pointing to the first sentence of the RL text: "How does the caterpillar feel at the beginning?") Student: "Scared." (Teacher, pointing to the last sentence: "How about at the end?") Student: "Not scared anymore."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can identify the beginning, middle, and end of a short text or story with a clear, sequential structure when given support.
Example: (Teacher points to pictures representing the RL text: caterpillar hiding, cocoon, butterfly flying) "Can you put these pictures in order? What happened first, second, last?"
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can with significant support, identify the beginning and end of a very simple story or text.
Example: (Teacher points to the first page of the RL text) "Where does the story start?" (Teacher points to the last page) "Where does the story end?"

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.5|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.6|5.text: In literary text, explain how a narrator’s or speaker’s point of view influences how events are described. (RL) In informational text, analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent. (RI)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.6|5.ee_text: With guidance and support, determine the point of view of a narrator (RL); compare two texts on the same topic (RI).

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can analyze how the point of view shapes not just what is told but how it is told, considering tone, style, and the narrator's reliability. In informational texts, I can evaluate the credibility of different perspectives, considering authors' backgrounds and potential biases.
Example (RL): "In Wonder, Auggie's use of humor and childish phrases shows us he's young, but it also makes us feel sympathetic towards him. The reader might wonder if Auggie's perspective is always accurate because he's sensitive about his appearance."
Example (RI): "The citizen's article focuses on the fear and hardship of the event, while the soldier's article talks about strategy and victory. The citizen's account might be more relatable, but the soldier might have a more complete understanding of the battle."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can explain how the narrator's or speaker's perspective shapes the reader's understanding of events in a story. In informational text, I can identify and analyze different perspectives on the same topic, noting similarities and differences.
Example (RL): "We see everything in Wonder through Auggie's eyes, so we understand why he's nervous about starting school. The author uses Auggie's point of view to make us feel what it's like to be different."
Example (RI): "Both articles talk about the same event, but they have different feelings about it. The citizen is scared, but the soldier is brave. This shows that people experience events differently."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify the narrator's perspective in a story and recognize that different characters might have different viewpoints. In informational text, I can recognize that different people can have different opinions on the same topic.
Example (RL): "The narrator in Wonder is Auggie, so we know what he's thinking and feeling. The other kids in his class probably see things differently than he does."
Example (RI): "The two articles disagree about what happened. The citizen thinks it was a disaster, but the soldier says they won the battle."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can identify the narrator or speaker in a story. In informational text, I can recognize that different people wrote the texts.
Example (RL): "The story is about Auggie. He is telling the story."
Example (RI): "These articles are written by different people. They have different names on them."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can with guidance, identify the point of view in a simple story and can find basic similarities between texts on the same topic.
Example: (Teacher: "Whose eyes are we seeing the story through?") Student: "The puppy's."
Example: (Teacher: "What is the same in both of these penguin paragraphs?") Student: "They both talk about penguins."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can with support, identify who is telling a simple story.
Example: (Teacher points to a picture of the puppy in the story) "Who is telling this story?"
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can with significant support and visual cues, recognize that who is telling the story.
Example: (Teacher points to a thought bubble above the puppy's head) "This story is told from inside the puppy's head. We know what the puppy is thinking."

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.6|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.7|5.text: Analyze how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning of literary and informational texts. (RI&RL)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.7|5.ee_text: Identify illustrations, tactual or multimedia elements that add to understanding of a text. (RI&RL)

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can analyze how specific visual and multimedia techniques (color, composition, sound, etc.) create effects and enhance meaning beyond the literal level. Can make connections between these choices and the creator's purpose.
Example: "The artist uses dark, shadowy illustrations during the Cyclops scene to create a feeling of suspense and danger. This choice emphasizes how terrifying the Cyclops is to Odysseus and his men."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can explain how visual and multimedia elements work together to contribute to the overall meaning or message of a text, providing evidence from the text.
Example: "The speech bubbles show us what the characters are saying, but the illustrations also show their emotions. When Odysseus comes up with a plan, his face looks determined in the picture."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify most visual and multimedia elements in a text and can explain how some of them connect to the meaning of the story.
Example: "I see that the artist used a lot of blue and green colors on this page. That might be because they are on an island."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can identify some visual and multimedia elements in a text but may not yet be able to explain how they connect to the meaning.
Example: "This page has words and pictures. I see a picture of a boat and a monster.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can identify specific visual elements in a text and I can explain how those elements help me understand the story better.
Example: "The picture shows Corduroy looking sad because he lost his button."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can identify visual elements in a text that directly represent what is happening in the story.
Example: (Teacher: "Point to the picture that shows Corduroy looking for his button.")
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can with support, identify a specific object or character within an illustration when directed.
Example: (Teacher: "Can you point to Corduroy on this page?")

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.7|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.8|5.text: Explain how claims in a text are supported by relevant reasons and evidence, identifying which reasons and evidence support which claims. (RI)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.8|5.ee_text: Identify the relationship between a specific point and supporting reasons in a text. (RI)

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can critically analyzes the effectiveness of an author's argument, evaluating the strength of evidence and recognizing the use of counterarguments and rebuttals. 
I can apply these skills to real-world situations.
Example: "The author claims that a four-day week improves student focus, but the study they cite only looked at test scores, not actual classroom behavior. This makes their evidence less convincing. They also don't address the concern about childcare for working parents, which weakens their argument."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can identify the central claim(s) in a text and explains how each piece of evidence supports specific points. 
I can distinguish between strong and weak evidence.
Example: "The author thinks a four-day week is better. They say that students will learn more because they'll be more rested. They did a study that showed scores went up when schools tried it."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify the main claim of a text and can recognize some of the evidence used to support it. I may struggle to explain the connection between evidence and claims consistently.
Example: "The article is about having a shorter school week. They talked about a study where kids did better on tests."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
Can pick out some statements that sound like claims (opinions or arguments) within a text and can identify some facts or details.
Example: "This part says that kids need more sleep. This part talks about a school that tried something different."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can identify a specific point an author is making and match it to a supporting reason or detail provided in a short text.
Example: (Teacher: "Why does the story say helmets are important?") Student: "Because when Max fell off his bike, his helmet protected his head."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can with support, identify a reason or detail within a short text that the author uses to support a point.
Example: (Teacher points to the sentence, "His helmet cracked, but Max's head was safe!") "What does this sentence tell us about why Max is okay?"
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can with significant support, identify a specific detail within a short text when prompted.
Example: (Teacher points to the picture of Max's cracked helmet) "What happened to the helmet in the story?"

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.8|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.9|5.text: Make informed judgments about quality of text; make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, identities, eras, and personal experiences. (RI&RL)
WI-CC-ELA|R.5.9|5.ee_text: Compare and contrast details gained from two texts and make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, identities, eras, personal events, or situations. (RI&RL)

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can evaluate the effectiveness of an author's craft and message while making insightful connections between texts, historical contexts, cultural perspectives, and personal experiences.
Example: "Both articles show how human actions threaten animals, but the elephant article is more effective because it uses stronger emotional appeals through vivid descriptions and personal stories. This reminds me of the documentary we watched about deforestation, which also highlighted the negative impact of human activity on wildlife."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can compare and contrasts how different texts approach similar themes or topics, making connections between texts, ideas, and personal experiences. I can analyze an author's purpose and point of view.
Example: "Both articles are about saving animals, but one is about elephants and the other is about sea turtles. They both talk about how important it is to protect these animals' habitats. This reminds me of when I visited the zoo and learned about endangered species."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can identify the main idea and supporting details in two texts and can make basic connections between them. I may identify some cultural references or connections to other familiar texts.
Example: "These stories are both about animals. The first one is about elephants, which are big, and the second one is about sea turtles, which live in the ocean. I remember reading another book about a turtle before."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can identify basic similarities between two texts, particularly related to two elements (ex. characters or topics). I can make simple connections to personal experiences.
Example: "Both of these stories are about animals trying to survive. That reminds me of my pet dog because he's always trying to find food."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can compare and contrast specific details from two short stories or texts. I can make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, or personal experiences.
Example: "In both stories, the main characters had to be brave. The boy in the bike story had to keep trying even though he fell down. The animals in the flood story had to work together to escape."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can with support, identify similar information presented in two short stories or texts on the same topic.
Example: (Teacher: "What do both stories tell us about what the characters had to do?") Student: "They both had to be brave."
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can with support, identify a basic similarity between two short stories or texts with similar topics.
Example: (Teacher: "What is similar about the characters in these two stories?") Student: "They are both animals."

WI-CC-ELA|R.5.9|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.1|5.text: Compose reflective, formal, and creative writing, which may happen simultaneously or independently, for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.
WI-CC-ELA|W.5.1|5.ee_text: With guidance and support, use drawing, dictating, or writing to compose writing for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can compose clear, well-organized, and engaging writing for a variety of purposes, adapting style and tone appropriately. I can effectively use evidence and reasoning to support claims and arguments. Demonstrates strong revision and editing skills.
Example (Persuasive): "Our class should visit the science museum because it offers hands-on exhibits that bring science to life. For example, the electricity exhibit allows students to experiment with circuits, which helps them understand the principles of electricity in a fun and memorable way."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can compose writing for different purposes (narrative, informational, persuasive) with clarity and organization. I can use evidence to support ideas and explanations. Revises and edits writing to improve clarity and flow.
Example (Narrative): "I was scared to try out for the soccer team, but my best friend encouraged me to be brave. When I finally stepped onto the field, I felt a surge of excitement. Even though I didn't make the team that year, I was proud of myself for trying."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can write with some clarity and organization, attempting to use different writing styles for different purposes.
I may use evidence to support writing inconsistently.
Example (Informational): "Elephants are really big animals. They live in Africa. They are endangered because people hunt them for their tusks. We need to protect them."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
Attempts to write for different purposes, but writing may lack clarity, organization, or consistent style. May struggle to use evidence effectively.
Example (Persuasive - with picture support): (Student draws a picture of a field trip destination) "I want to go here. It will be fun."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can with guidance and support, compose simple writing for different purposes, using basic sentences and vocabulary. 
I may use pictures and symbols to support writing. Can participate in the revision process with support.
Example (Low-Stakes): (Student draws a picture of a cat) "This is my cat, Mittens. She is soft and likes to play with string."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
I can with support, express an opinion about a topic or text and provide a simple reason to support that opinion. 
I may use pictures and symbols to enhance writing.
Example (Opinion): (Teacher: "What did you think of the story?") Student: "I liked the story. The dog was funny." (Student draws a picture of a dog with its tongue out.)
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can with significant support, introduce a topic or text and state a simple opinion about it.
I may use pictures and symbols as the primary form of communication.
Example (Topic Introduction): (Teacher shows a picture of a lion) "This is a lion. Do you like lions?" Student: "Yes!"

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.1|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.a|5.text: Write text in a variety of modes. a. Opinion pieces that support a point of view about a topic or text clearly, state an opinion, and create an organizational structure in which ideas are logically ordered to support facts, details, and the writer's purpose.
WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.a|5.ee_text: With guidance and support, use writing, dictation and/or drawing to compose: a. Opinion pieces in which they clearly state an opinion about a topic or text and include some reasons to support that opinion.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can write a persuasive opinion piece that effectively argues my point of view using strong evidence, reasoning, and by anticipating counterarguments.
Ex: "School uniforms may seem like a good idea for promoting unity, but they actually stifle students' self-expression and creativity. When we can choose our own clothing, we can express our individuality and personal style. Schools can promote unity through other means, such as school spirit days or shared activities, without sacrificing students' freedom of choice."
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can write a well-organized opinion piece that clearly states my opinion and supports it with reasons, evidence, and transition words.
Ex: "I believe students should be allowed to have cell phones in school. First, cell phones can be valuable learning tools. Students can use them for research, to access educational apps, and to take notes. Secondly, cell phones can provide a sense of security for students, allowing them to contact their families in case of an emergency."
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can write a paragraph or two about a topic, stating my opinion clearly and attempting to use evidence.
Ex: "I think school uniforms are a bad idea. Kids should be able to wear what they want. It's not fair to make everyone look the same. Uniforms are boring."
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can write a few sentences about a topic, but my opinion may be unclear or my writing may lack organization.
Ex: "School uniforms? Some kids want to wear different clothes. Make it more fun."
descriptors.ee_at_target:
Composes simple opinion pieces, clearly stating an opinion and providing a few reasons with some detail, using pictures, symbols, or dictation to support writing.
Example: (Student draws a picture of children playing on a sunny playground.) "I like to play outside. The sun feels good, and I can run around."
descriptors.ee_approaching:
With prompting and support, can state an opinion about a topic or text and provide a simple reason to justify that opinion, possibly using pictures and symbols to enhance communication.
Example: (Teacher: "Where do you like to play - inside or outside?") Student: "Outside! It's more fun." (Student draws a smiley face next to the word "outside.")
descriptors.ee_emerging:
With significant support, can express a preference or opinion about a topic, possibly relying primarily on nonverbal communication or single words to convey their stance.
Example: (Teacher points to a picture of a playground and a picture of a living room.) "Which one do you like better?" Student points to the picture of the playground.

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.a|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.b|5.text: Informative text that introduces a topic clearly, use topic- and genre-specific language to provide a general observation, focus, and group related information logically. Include formatting (e.g., headings), illustrations, and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension and to link ideas within and across categories of information.
WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.b|5.ee_text: Informative/Explanatory text in which they introduce a topic and provide some facts, details, and/or multimedia content about a predetermined or self chosen topic.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can write engaging and informative texts that delve deeply into a topic, using precise language, varied sentence structures, and thoughtfully chosen multimedia elements to enhance the reader's understanding. My writing demonstrates a strong command of language and a sophisticated understanding of the topic.
Ex: A student researches and writes a compelling report on renewable energy sources. They use technical vocabulary accurately, incorporate data and statistics to support their claims, and include graphs and diagrams to illustrate different energy production methods. They also effectively compare and contrast various renewable energy options, analyzing their benefits and drawbacks.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can write well-organized informative texts that clearly introduce a topic, provide relevant facts and details, and use headings and multimedia to enhance comprehension.
Ex: A student writes a report about the rainforest ecosystem. They include sections on different layers of the rainforest, the plants and animals found in each layer, and the importance of rainforest conservation. They use headings to organize information and include relevant images of rainforest life.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
I can write informative texts that introduce a topic and provide some basic facts and details. My writing may be less organized, and my use of multimedia may be limited.
Ex: A student writes a report about the giraffe, mentioning its height, diet, and habitat. The information is present but may lack detailed explanations or smooth transitions between ideas.
descriptors.cc_emerging:
I can write or dictate a few sentences about a topic with support, possibly using pictures or symbols to convey information.
Ex: A student, with prompting and support from the teacher, writes a few sentences about a lion ("Lions are big. They have fur. They roar.") and draws a picture of a lion.
descriptors.ee_at_target:
I can write or dictate informative texts that introduce a topic clearly and provide some supporting facts, details, and/or multimedia elements.
Ex: A student chooses to write about their favorite animal, a dog. They write a paragraph describing dogs, including details about their care, and draw a picture of a dog.
descriptors.ee_approaching:
With prompting and support, I can contribute facts, details, or other information related to a topic, possibly using pictures and symbols to support communication.
Ex: In a small group led by the teacher, a student contributes information about a cat ("Cats meow. They like to sleep.") when prompted and draws a picture of a cat on a shared piece of chart paper.
descriptors.ee_emerging:
I can express interest in a topic and, with significant support, contribute simple information or preferences.
Ex: When shown a picture of a rainforest, a student points excitedly to a monkey and vocalizes, prompting the teacher to write "monkey" on a graphic organizer.

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.b|5.source: Awsaj EE ELA New Standards 2025 V1 Complete (school sheet, K-5)

WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.c|5.text: Convey events, real or imagined, through narrative or short stories which orients a reader by establishing a real or imagined situation and introducing a narrator and characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally. Use narrative techniques, such as dialogue, description, and pacing, to develop experiences and events or show the responses of characters to situations.
WI-CC-ELA|W.5.2.c|5.ee_text: Convey events, real or imagined and narrate a single event or several loosely linked events. Include some details regarding what happened and tell about the events in the order in which they occurred.

descriptors.cc_advanced:
I can craft engaging narratives that immerse the reader in the story world. My writing demonstrates skillful use of dialogue, description, pacing, and other narrative techniques to develop characters, plot, and mood.
Ex: A student writes a suspenseful story about discovering a hidden door, using vivid imagery to describe the secret passageway and incorporating internal monologue to reveal the main character's growing curiosity and apprehension.
descriptors.cc_at_target:
I can write narratives that are easy to follow and understand. I can use dialogue, description, and pacing to develop characters and events, showing how characters respond to situations.
Ex: A student writes a story about finding a hidden door that leads to a room full of fascinating old toys. The story includes dialogue between the main character and their friend, descriptions of the toys, and a clear sequence of events.
descriptors.cc_approaching:
